en: For the Sword Mudrā of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata:

join the two hands at the heart with palms together; bend the middle joints of the two index fingers so they touch each other crosswise, and place the two thumbs side by side, pressing down on the upper joints of the two index fingers in the shape of a sword. Upon forming this mudrā, immediately—

Visualize within your own heart an eight-petaled lotus flower. Within the flower, imagine the syllable *ĀḤ* emitting golden light in resonance with the mudrā; contemplate that syllable *ĀḤ* as realizing that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning.
Then recite the mantra:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ vīra hūṃ khaṃ*. Next, recite the mantra eight times and, using the mudrā as before, consecrate five places on one's own body—namely, the forehead, the right shoulder, the left shoulder, the heart, and the throat—and finally release it over the crown of the head.

The Mudrā of the Sovereign of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa: First, join the palms. Interlace the two ring fingers and the two little fingers, right over left, so that their tips meet within the palms. Straighten the two middle fingers, bending their first joints so that their heads touch like the shape of a sword. Insert the two thumbs into the palms. Extend the two index fingers straight, bending them to press against the nails of the thumbs so that their tips touch. This is called the Fundamental Mudrā of the Sovereign of the Uṣṇīṣa.
The verse says:
This mudrā is the Mahāmudrā, known as the Tathāgatoṣṇīṣa; having just bound it, one becomes equal to the World-Honored One.
The mantra of Uṣṇīṣacakravartin:

*Namo samantabhadramunīndrāya oṃ.* For anyone who makes a request for whatever matter they seek, one should here append the Peacock King Dhāraṇī: *būroṃ*. Next, perform the Seal of the Peacock King (*mayūrarāja-mudrā*): Interlace the two hands with the palms facing inward; extend the thumbs and ring fingers straight up with their tips touching, and likewise extend the middle fingers and little fingers straight up with their sides touching. Thus the seal is formed.
Recite the mantra three or seven times, reciting it in conjunction with the Cakravartin King; one should add these mantra syllables.

The mantra is recited as follows: *Oṃ madyula karaṇḍe svāhā*. If one is performing the ordinary recitation of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King mantra, one must separately recite the Peacock King (Mayūrajāla) mantra and also separately recite this method for adding the supplementary phrases. This must be personally transmitted orally by a master (ācārya); it is known only by those who practice yoga.
The Vajra-liberation Mantra:
"Oṃ vajramuṣṭi muḥ. The Mantra of the Bodhisattva Parṇaśavarī:
"Oṃ padmaśavari hūṃ phaṭ. The Mantra of Tathāgata Jñānaketu:
*Namo āśvastaśrītināṃ samyaksaṃbuddhakuṭiṃ namo oṃ kīñjāna vabhase dṛdṛ hūṃ.* The Great Compassionate Heart Mantra:
*Oṃ padmaca kṣaraṃ khaga nadra ni la khaṃṭa siddhya siddhya hūṃ.* The Tārā Bodhisattva Mantra:
Oṃ tathāgatāśayāśayāśaya svāhā. The mantra of the Tathāgata’s kāṣāya:
Oṃ vajrasattvādhiṣṭhāna dṛḍha vajra svāhā. The One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa.
“Bhruṃ Oṃ” (the three syllables combined): the Vajra Life-Extending Mantra:
“Oṃ Vajrayuṣe Svāhā. The Vajra Life Mantra: “Oṃ Jñāna Vajrayu. The Vajrarāja Mantra:
“Oṃ ṭa ki hūṃ ja. This is the mantra of Sitātapatrā-uṣṇīṣa.
“Oṃ ma ma hūṃ khaṃ. This is the mantra of Vairocana Buddha.
“Oṃ bhruḥ a vi ra hūṃ khaṃ. This is the mantra of Tejorāśi-uṣṇīṣa.
“Oṃ kha kha kha khe kha khe hūṃ hūṃ jvala ra prajvala jvala ra prajvala jvala ra tiṣṭha tiṣṭha hṛditi svāhā. This is the mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:
“Oṃ hrīḥ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the Heart Mantra of Amoghapāśa: “Oṃ amoghapāśahṛdaya hūṃ phaṭ. This is the Gaganagañja Pūrṇamantra:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatādhipatirājāgrya hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ trailokyam. The Samaya-mantra of Ākāśagarbha:
Oṃ vajraratna hūṃ. The Mantra of Ākāśagarbha: Oṃ gagana-sambhava-vajra hoḥ oṃ aḥ hūṃ. The Karma-mantra of Ākāśagarbha:
Oṃ vajra-ratna-haṃ. This is the eight-syllable mantra of Mañjuśrī.
A-vi-ra-hūṃ kha-ca-la-taṃ. This is the six-syllable mantra of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Oṃ vajra-keta-nā-maḥ. This is the mantra of the Peacock King (Mayūravidyārāja).
*Namo ratnatrayāya hūṃ.* The *dhāraṇī* of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is:
*Oṃ samantabhadra svāhā.* The mantra for removing poison is: *Oṃ a-nar-bha-nar-na-ga-ma-ri-ni hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.* The mantra of the Bodhicitta:
“Oṃ jñīptamatabhānyami. The following dhāraṇī says: “Oṃ vajracittasamayehūṃ. This is the Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Dhāraṇī.
*Namo ārya-mañjuśrīye bhagavate tadyathā jaye jaye jayāya mahe mahā-he svāhā.* The mantra for assisting the empowerment of the Uṣṇīṣa to bring rain:
*Oṃ bhrūṃ ānandana-garaka-bhye hūṃ phaṭ.* The Vajra-mahācakra-dhāraṇī says: *Namo maṃtraye jyeṣṭha-kā...*
South: *tad* (1), *gata* (2), *oṃ* (3),
*vīra* (4), *vīra* (5), *mahācakrara* (6), *vajri* (7), *sata* (8), *sata* (9), *sa* (10).
raṭe saraṭe traḍaye traḍaye vidamati saṃpanni traṃ maditi siddhagiri-taḥ.
*Juh-yen* (Entrustment): *svāhā hāḥ*. The Mantra for Repentance and the Extinction of Sins:
*oṃ sarvapāpanāśana vajrāya svāhā hāḥ*. Verses for Bathing the Image:
"I now bathe all the Tathāgatas, The assembly adorned with pure wisdom and merit;
May all beings in the five turbidities Swiftly realize the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgata."
The verse for resolving doubts:
"The Buddhas now act for you to resolve and eliminate the darkness of ignorance;
just as the King of Physicians in the world, so too am I now."

Next, form the Buddha-Eye Mudrā: join the two hands in *añjali*; bend both thumbs double and insert them into the palms; place the two index fingers against the backs of the first joints of the two middle fingers, like two eyes facing one another. This is called the Buddha-Eye Mudrā.
Once it has been accomplished, empower the five places—namely, the forehead, the right shoulder, the left shoulder, the heart, and the throat—and scatter [the remains] upon the crown of the head.
Recite the mantra as follows:
*Namo sarvatathāgatādhipati-vairocana-prabhā-samaya-mūrti-vajra | Oṃ ru ru saparu jvala tiṣṭha siddhārtho me sarvārthasādhane svāhā.* Next, bind the sword mudrā of Vairocana Tathāgata.

Place both hands at the heart with palms joined; bend the middle joints of the two index fingers so that they touch each other crosswise, and place the two thumbs side by side, pressing down on the upper joints of the two index fingers in the shape of a sword.

Having bound this mudrā, one should immediately visualize an eight-petaled lotus within one’s own heart. Within that lotus, one should imagine the letter *A* emitting golden light in resonance with the mudrā; by contemplating that letter *A*, one realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn from the very beginning.
Then recite the mantra:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ viraha hūṃ khaṃ*. Next, recite the mantra eight times and, using the mudrā as before, empower five places on one’s own body—namely, the forehead, the right shoulder, the left shoulder, the heart, and the throat—and finally release the mudrā upon the crown of the head.
Next, using the heart-mantra of Kuṇḍalī, protect all objects thoroughly to remove impurities and purify them.
Recite the mantra:

"Oṃ āḥ mṛte hūṃ phaṭ. With the right hand, take up pure water, empower it seven times with the mantra, and sprinkle it upon the cleansing powder and other substances; they will thereby become purified.

Next, recite the root mantra of Kuṇḍalī and perform the secret mudrā to scoop up water. For this mudrā, extend the wisdom arm (right hand) flat; bend the second joints of the *dharaṇī* (ring) and *praṇidhāna* (little) fingers and insert them into the palm. With the *prajñā* (middle) finger, pinch the upper joints of those two [bent] fingers. Form fists with the wisdom finger at the side of the *dharaṇī* joint and the power (*bala*) finger at the side of the *praṇidhāna* joint. Using this mudrā, scoop up water and empower it by reciting the root mantra seven times. Thereafter, loosen the garment and bathe as you please.
The mantra is: Namo ratnatrayāya namo śrīvajrapāṇaye.
VAJRA KURU SHTAṬI SHTAṬA | VANDA VANDA | HANA HANA | AMR̥TE HŪṂ PHAṬ ||
*Ṭa* (half-syllable) *svāhā*. Regarding the general method for bathing, there is a threefold classification of washing;
one must know the sequence and order: from the feet to the navel is the lower portion (*adhobhāga*); from the navel to the neck is called the middle portion (*madhyabhāga*);
and from the neck to the crown of the head is the upper portion (*ūrdhvabhāga*).
One should first wash the lower part thoroughly; then, having cleansed the hands with soap-nut and cleansing powder, one should next wash the middle part;
then, having again cleansed the hands, one should pour [water] over the upper part.

This sutra states: "Whenever you bathe, you should maintain a tranquil and single-minded recitation of the mantra without distraction. You must not engage in laughter or frivolous, meaningless conversation; do not look at private parts, nor should you harbor thoughts of sensual desire for men or women. Bathe solely for the purpose of removing impurities, without the intention of adorning the body. Maintain mindfulness with a single mind, following the sequence according to the Dharma to protect yourself. You should not scold or rebuke those who are superior or inferior; if there are matters that do not go as you wish, you should instruct them with a compassionate heart and kind words."
Having thus completed the ritual bath according to the instructions and the Dharma, one should next perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Using this mantra to empower a pure flask, one should pour its contents over the crown of the head.
The mantra is as follows:
"Oṃ kha-kha-ri-ri hūṃ phaṭ. If one performs the self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), it is sufficient to recite the mantra twenty-one times;
however, if consecrating a companion or a disciple who knows the Dharma, one must complete one hundred and eight recitations.
As if there were no vase or person present, simply scoop up water with this mudrā; for every scoop of water, empower it by reciting the mantra seven times.
Having thus empowered the water three times according to the ritual, pour it over one’s own head.

For this mudrā, interlace the fingers of the wisdom-hand (right) over the palms of the dharma-hand (left), with the thumbs tucked into the palms. Bend the index fingers of the precept-hand (left) together and place them crossed over the top. Straighten the thumbs of the patience-hand (right) and touch their tips together. Bend the middle fingers of the effort-hand (left) and rest them upon the backs of the knuckles of the patience-hand's thumbs. Finally, straighten both the ring fingers and little fingers; thus it is formed. This is called the Consecration Mudrā (*abhiṣeka-mudrā*).
Next, using the previously mentioned Mahāsamaya mantra and its corresponding mudrā as before, empower the five places of one’s own body as before.
Then, using the Kuṇḍalī heart-mantra as before, scoop up water, empower it, and sprinkle it upon the garment you are wearing to purify it; thereafter, take it up and put it on.

One must continue to recite auspicious verses (*śrī-gāthā*) without interruption until reaching one's seat; there, with the thought that one is paying homage and making offerings to all Buddhas with this purified body and mind, one enters the maṇḍala to perform the worship, as described in the Great Teachings.

Based on the *Susiddhikara Sūtra* and the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra Brief Commentary*, I shall explain the method for purifying the three karmas through empowerment against defilements caused by contact. Regarding the purification of the three karmas: at times the body may be defiled by contact, the mouth may engage in eating or speaking various miscellaneous words, or the mind may contemplate matters that are not beneficial; these are all termed impurities of the three karmas. Therefore, one must employ this dhāraṇī and correct contemplation to empower them, so that sinful stains are eliminated and the actions of body, speech, and mind are swiftly purified.
The mantra is:
Oṃ svabhāva-śuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāva-śuddho ’haṃ. Recite this mantra seven times; more is even better.
This mantra is capable of removing all defilements of the karmas of body, speech, and mind, such that they all attain purity.

While reciting it correctly, one should enter this yoga-contemplation and reflect: "The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure; it is merely obscured by false, adventitious afflictions. Having lost sight of the correct principle, there arise inverted, deluded attachments to the fruits of good and evil karma."

I now enter the inconceivable contemplation of the equality of the Dharma-realm, thoroughly understanding that all afflictions, transgressions, and defilements are fundamentally pure. Furthermore, through the inconceivable power of dhāraṇī and by the power of the corresponding empowerment of the supernatural faculties shared by all Buddhas, all afflictions and deluded thoughts are purified at that very moment.

Why is this? Because one realizes that those afflictions arise from delusion and lack intrinsic nature; being like an illusion or a dream, they are fundamentally pure. By performing this yoga of correct contemplation and secret empowerment, there is no evil karma that is not purified.
In this sutra, it is called the "Secret Inner Method of Bathing.
Regarding the methods for purifying defilements, there are two kinds of defilement:

first, when one is about to enter a place of physical defilement, one should recite the wrathful mantra of Ucchuṣma seven times. This can expel all foulness and evil so that they do not adhere to the body or mind. By empowering the body with this, one becomes like a wrathful Vajra, such that Vināyakas cannot find an opportunity to cause harm.
The mantra of the Wrathful King Ucchuṣma is: *Oṃ kuruḍa na hūṃ jaḥ*.

Secondly, if a person who has long maintained the recitation suddenly and unconsciously becomes defiled—whether by eating impure food, wearing impure clothing, or being assaulted by defilement—and perceives their own body and mind to be uneasy, they must immediately rub and wash a gold, silver, or white porcelain vessel with ash-water. Taking a small amount of fresh, newly drawn water, they should empower it seven times, twenty-one times, or one hundred and eight times with the Mañjuśrī (Muṇḍarī) mantra and then drink it; at that moment, the affliction will be pacified instantly, like snow melting in hot water.
This mantra is named "Dissolving Impurities through Touch.
These two mantras are fully set forth in the *Muṇḍarī-vidhi*.
The mantra says:
*Namo ratnatrayāya namo vajrakrodhāya | Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ tiṣṭha tiṣṭha bandha bandha hana hana āmṛte hūṃ phaṭ svāhā* | This is the Samaya-mudrā of the Heart of the Buddha Family.

Forming fists by interlacing the fingers of the hands representing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within the ten *pāramitās*, extend the thumbs (*dhyāna*) and middle fingers (*prajñā*) side-by-side; having completed the mudrā, visualize all Buddhas pervading space, recite the mantra three times, and release the mudrā over the crown of the head.
Recite the mantra:
Oṃ kīṃ karaṃ svāhā. Next, form the Samaya-mudrā of the Lotus Family.
Following the previous heart-mudrā of the Buddha Family, bend the *jñāna-aṅgulī* (middle finger) into the palm and extend the *dhyānāṅgulī* (ring finger) straight upward.

Having formed the mudrā, visualize that to the right of all Tathāgatas there is Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva together with his retinue; then recite the mantra three times and release the mudrā over the right side of the head.
Recite the mantra:
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā. Next, form the Samaya-mudrā of the Heart of the Vajra Family.

Following the preceding heart-mudrā of the Buddha family, bend the *dhyāna-pāramitā* (ring finger) inward into the palm and extend the *prajñā-pāramitā* (middle finger) straight upward. Visualize that to the left of all Tathāgatas there is the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi together with his retinue; then recite the mantra three times and release the mudrā over the left side of the crown.
Recite the mantra:
Oṃ vajra ṭīk ca svāhā. Next, perform the armor-binding mudrā for protecting the body.

Visualize the dhyāna and prajñā pāramitās as feathers extending across the palm; with the śīla, kṣānti, and dāna pāramitās, form a fist. Once the mudrā has been completed, perform the empowerment upon five locations—namely, the forehead, the right shoulder, the left shoulder, the heart, and the throat—which are known as the five locations.
The mantra for protecting the body is:
Oṃ bhūr jvala hūṃ. This is the mudrā for expelling obstacles by the One-Syllable Cakravartin.

Interlace the left and right index, ring, and little fingers, placing the right over the left and tucking them into the palms to form fists. Bend both thumbs double and tuck them into the palms. Hold the middle fingers straight upright with their tips touching one another. Once the mudrā is formed, rotate it three times counter-clockwise above the crown of the head to expel obstructors, and three times clockwise to establish protection; wherever the mind reaches, the boundaries of the sacred precinct are thereby established.

This mudrā can destroy all obstacles to the rites of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣas. Should any evil devas, nāgas, or the eight classes of beings—including yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and vināyakas—see this mudrā, they shall all flee in terror and be driven away.
Recite the mantra:
*Namaḥ samantabhadranām oṃ nṛoṃ maṃ bhaṃ svāhā*. Next, the mantra for offering the arghya is: *Namaḥ samantabhadranām gagana-samama svāhā*.
Holding the vessel with both hands at the forehead, kneel on the calves and recite the mantra three times to offer the arghya and bathe the assembly of holy ones.
Next, bind the seal of universal offering:

*Namo samantabhadramūrtaye sarvathā khaṃ udanate sphara hīṃ gagaṇa khaṃ svāhā*. By the power of this mantra, clouds and oceans of all kinds of lamps flow forth, making offerings to all Tathāgatas and the assembly of holy beings.

Furthermore, one should visualize banners, pennants, canopies, nets, necklaces, garments, silks, and other such objects pervading the boundless dharma-realm of the ocean-like clouds of offerings. With words of sincerity, one recites these sublime verses to offer praise:
"By the power of my merit, by the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment, and by the power of the dharma-realm, I abide in universal offering."
Next, bind the Buddha’s Great Compassionate Protection Mudrā.

Interlace the ten fingers to form a crescent moon; join the thumbs, middle fingers, and ring fingers upright and touching one another. Having completed the binding of the mudrā, seal the heart, forehead, and throat, then release the mudrā over the crown of the head.
Recite the mantra:
Oṃ mudrā-maitrī-vajra-rakṣa haṃ svāhā. Next, perform the Buddha-Eye Mudrā (Buddhalocanā-mudrā).

Join the two hands in *añjali*; bend both thumbs inward into the palms; place the tips of the two index fingers against the backs of the first joints of the two middle fingers, like two eyes facing each other. This is called the Buddha-Eye Mudrā (*buddhanetra-mudrā*).
Once it is accomplished, empower the five places—namely, the forehead, the right shoulder, the left shoulder, the heart, and the throat—and perform the mudrā of scattering upon the crown of the head.
The mantra is as follows:
*Namo sarvatathāgatādhipatividyārāja-samyaksambuddhāya | Oṃ ruru saparu jvalara tiṣṭha siddharuḍhya svāhā.* Next, form the seal of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King.

First, join the palms. Interlace the two left ring fingers and the two left little fingers with the right pressing over the left, inserting them into the palms. Straighten the two middle fingers, bending their first joints so that their tips touch like the shape of a sword. Insert the two thumbs into the palms, extend the two index fingers levelly, and bend them to press against the nail-tips of the two thumbs so that their tips touch. This is called the Root Seal of the Cakravartin.
The verse says:
"This mudrā is the Great Mudrā, known as the Tathāgata’s Crown.
As soon as it is bound, one becomes identical to the World-Honored One."
The mantra is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ*. For anyone who makes a request for all things sought, one should here append the Mahāmāyūrī Dhāraṇī: *būroṃ*. Next is the Mahāmāyūrī Mudrā.

Interlace the two hands with the palms facing inward, extend the thumbs and wisdom-fingers (*tarjanī*) straight upward so that their tips touch, and likewise extend the middle fingers (*madhyamā*) straight upward so that they stand side by side touching; thus the mudrā is formed.
Recite the mantra three or seven times, reciting it in conjunction with the *Uṣṇīṣacakravartin*, and these mantra syllables should be added.
The mantra is recited as follows:

Oṃ mayūra-kalānte svāhā. If one is habitually reciting the mantra of the One-Syllable Cakravartin, it is necessary to separately recite the mantra of the Peacock King (Mayūrarāja) and also separately recite this method of adding the phrase. This must be personally transmitted by oral precept from the ācārya; it is known only by those who practice yoga.
Furthermore, the ritual method for the altar of praying for rain is explained:
if there is a severe drought and one wishes to pray for rain, construct an altar in an open space;
clear away tiles, rubble, and all impure things; set up a blue curtain and hang blue banners; and smear the ground with fragrant mud to prepare it.
On one side of the altar, within the altar, draw a pond of the seven treasures; within the pond, draw the palace of the Sāgara Nāgarāja.
Within that nāga palace, depict the form of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni dwelling and preaching the Dharma.
To the right of the Buddha, paint the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; to the left of the Buddha, paint the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and others as his attendants. Regarding the Buddha...
To the right of the front, paint the Dragon King Cakravartimaṇḍala, Lord of the Trichiliocosm;
to the left of the Buddha’s front, paint the two Dragon Kings Nanda and Upananda. At the four corners of the altar, use cow dung (gomaya) to paint a dragon king in each;
in the eastern direction, paint one dragon king with three heads, measuring three cubits in height.
Surrounded by his retinue;
furthermore, in the south, paint a nāga king with five heads on a single body, measuring five cubits in length, surrounded by his various attendants;
furthermore, in the west, paint a nāga king with seven heads on a single body, measuring seven cubits, surrounded by his various attendants.

Furthermore, in the northern direction, one should paint a nāga king with nine heads on a single body, measuring nine cubits in length, surrounded by his retinue, all within dense, dark blue-black clouds.

The lower half of their bodies were like those of serpents with tails submerged in the pond, while the upper half of their bodies took the form of bodhisattvas; all emerged from the pond with palms joined in homage.

Place four vases of pure water at the four corners of the mandala; according to one's capacity, provide offerings of food, drink, fruits, and so forth, all of which should be deep blue in color. Arrange these offerings with clean cloth, burn incense, and scatter blue flowers.
All items used within the *maṇḍala* (place of practice) should be made blue in color.
As for those who pray for rain: if they are ordained *bhikṣus*, they should be fully endowed with the *vinaya* discipline;
if they are laypersons, they should receive the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*).

When performing the ritual, one should consume the "three white foods" and bathe daily in fragrant water while wearing fresh, clean blue robes. Facing the west at the altar, one should prepare a seat of blue materials; then, having anointed the hands with incense, one should first perform the empowerment of the Three Mysteries to protect oneself and the altar. Place this *Mahāmegha Sūtra* upon the table, and with great compassion arising for all sentient beings, sincerely invoke the empowerment of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, reciting this *Mahāmegha Sūtra* with devotion day and night.
Whether it be two, three, or even up to seven people, they should take turns reciting the sutra so that the sound of the chanting does not cease.
During times of severe drought, if one recites this *Mahāmegha Sūtra* according to the Dharma for one day, two days, or even up to seven days, sweet rain will certainly fall.
If calamities are severe and there is no rain, performing the rite again will cause rain to fall.
Even if the great ocean should exceed its limits or overstep its tides, by relying on this sūtra to perform the ritual and recite it, there shall be nothing that does not respond.

Understanding what should be done, one should make a vow that the merit arising from reading this scripture be dedicated to all the nāgas, praying that they may all be freed from suffering and hardship, generate the unsurpassed bodhicitta, and pour down sweet rain for the sake of all sentient beings. This refers to the places where the secret scriptures are kept, located away from villages, towns, and the like.
The Vajra-liberation mantra:
“Oṃ vajramuṣṭi muḥ. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Parṇaśavarī:
“Oṃ padmaśavari hūṃ phaṭ. The mantra of the Tathāgata Jñānolkā:
*Namo āśasti-namaskāra-samyaksambuddha-gocitre | Oṃ kīñjanavāsasi-dhāri hūṃ* The Great Compassionate Heart-Mantra:
*Oṃ padmacakra-śaṅkha-kha-ga-na-siddhye hūṃ* The Heart-Mantra of Amitāyus Tathāgata: *Oṃ amṛtatejā-hara hūṃ* The Mantra of Tārā Bodhisattva:
Oṃ tathāgatāśaya tathāgatāśaya tathāgata svāhā. The mantra for the Tathāgata’s kāṣāya:
Oṃ kṣayasattvadhātucittasamatātmaja vajra svāhā. The *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*’s abbreviated ritual for recitation:
I bow my head to the one of unimpeded wisdom, The son born from the mind of the Secret Teaching.
Relying upon that sūtra, one gathers these auxiliary practices;
the practitioner of mantra first abides in the vow of equality,
with both the secret speech and the secret body, and subsequently performs the practice of correspondence.

The Samaya Mantra: As for the mudrā, it consists of joining the palms at the level of the wheels [the thumbs and little fingers], extending both index fingers (the two *śūnyatās*) upward, and placing them upon five locations:
the crown of the head, the shoulders, and the heart, with the final placement added at the throat.
Next, regarding the *Acalakalpa* (the *Acārya-guhya*), it is said that since this method of recitation is entirely identical to the version currently in circulation, it has been abbreviated here.

As for the eight grammatical cases (*vibhakti*), they are: the nominative (*kartṛ*), accusative (*karman*), instrumental (*karaṇa*), dative (*sampradāna*), ablative (*apādāna*), genitive (*saṃbandha*), locative (*adhikaraṇa*), and vocative (*sambodhana*).
Furthermore, regarding "the sound of essence" (*tīti-śabda*), it refers to designations such as "Bodhisattva Mahāsattva," which are calls based on one's essential nature.

Second, regarding "the sound of activity" (*karma-śabda*), it refers to the sound of activity arising from the Bodhisattva’s prior practice of the contemplation of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-vipaśyanā*).
Third, regarding the term "instrument": how does a bodhisattva practice the contemplation of non-apprehension? It is by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*; this is the meaning of the term "instrument."
Fourth, regarding the sound of the purpose: for what purpose does one practice? It means practicing for the sake of delivering all sentient beings;

this is the sound of the purpose. Fifth, regarding the sound of the source: from what does one practice? It means that because the Buddhas appear in the world and expound the True Dharma, it is from this sound that one practices.
Sixth, regarding that which pertains to the sound (*śabda*): "Whose non-attainment? and "the non-attainment of all phenomena"—this is what pertains to the sound.

Seventh, regarding that which relies upon the sound: "In what does one practice? relying upon the three stages of worthiness (*tri-piṭaka*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), etc.—this is what relies upon the sound.
8. Regarding "vocative sounds" (*āhvāna*): this refers to the names and terms used for calling out mentioned above; these constitute vocative sounds.
Below this, there are six types of *vigraha* (analytical explanations) of compound terms; as they are entirely identical to the common literary conventions in circulation, they are omitted here.
Included herein is the *Brief Ritual for the Recitation of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery.
This is also entirely identical to the version currently circulating in the world, and for that reason, it has been abbreviated here.
The *Mārīcī-sūtra*, in one fascicle, is likewise abbreviated here.
Next are the samaya mantras of the thirty-seven deities of the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-tantra*, listed here in their proper sequence; now they shall be abbreviated once more.
From the *Vajraśekhara-yogamahātantrarāja-sūtra*, the praises of the sixteen great bodhisattvas: Vajrapāṇi:
*vajrasattvamaha-sattva-vajrasarvātma-tathāgatābhisamitavajra-niyatavajra-dharmānāmodyate* Vajrarāja:

*vajrarāgāsuvamdhigirivajrakūṣmāṇḍatakhagatāmukhara-javajranitya-vajrakarṣaṇanamostute* Vajra-Love: "O Vajra-Love, you who bind with the vajra of passion, O you who possess the vajra of the *kūṣmāṇḍas*, you who go through the sky, homage to you, the eternal vajra who draws [all beings]!"
*vajrarāgamo hasaukuya vajra vana vaśaṅkara rāgama rāgakama mahāvajra cāpa nāmuṣṭi* Vajra-joy:
*vajrasattvasuvajragaraya vajra-dhūṣṭima-hāra-te pramum-ni-ya-raja vajra-hrīḥsa-namo-svaste* Vajraratna:
VAJRA-RATNA-SU-VAJRĀLITA VAJRA-KAŚAMA-MOHA-MO-NI Ā KAŚA-GHOPA VAJRA-JYA VAJRA-GHOṢA-NĀMA-MUDRĪTĀ. Vajraprabha:
VAJRA-TI-JA-MA-HA-JVALA-VAJRA-SŪRYA-NAMA-PRAVĀRṢMI-MA-HATI-JA-VAJRA-PRABHĀNA-MO. [The Sanskrit and Chinese equivalents for the preceding are as above; those below are all abbreviated. Vajradhvaja:
*vajra-ketu-sarvātman-vajra-dvaja-sudṛśya-krīḍana-ketu-mahāvajra-jaye...* The Vajra-Laughter:
“Vajra hā samahāhaḥ svavajra-smita-tama-hanabuddha-pratiti-pramunitaya vajra-prati... Vajradharma:
*vajra-dharma-svastyayana-vajra-bhāṣa-svadhā-kara-lokī-śvara-su-vajra-kṣaṇa-vajra-niṣṭhā...* Vajratīkṣṇa:
“Vajratīkṣṇaya dha vajra-kūṣmāṇḍa-hayūdvatama ca śrī-vajragarbha-nirjara vajramūrti... Vajrahetu:
"Vajra-he-tu-ma-ha-maṇa-vajra-ja-kar-ma-ha-nā-ya-su-pravardha-nā-vajra-jruta-dha-ta-vajra-maṇa... Vajra Speech:

"VAJRA-SAṂDHĪ-SUVA-NI-KṢA VAJRA-MAṆḌABHŪTA-MOKṢA VAJRA-MUKHA-STYAGARA-SAMAYANA VAJRA-MUCI... Herein are the mantras of various deities; they are not employed at present. As they are roughly identical to the dhāraṇīs and spells currently circulating in the world, they have been omitted here.
Regarding the extensive version of the Great Vairocana Sword Mudrā, it was bestowed by Preceptor Huiguo upon the Master’s return to China.
As for the abbreviated version, it was composed by the Minister of Monks Saichō (Shōnō Sōjō). Such is the tradition of its transmission.
In recent years, many editions have been seen, yet the errors in transcription are not few; therefore, I have collated these against the printed versions so that readers may easily perceive them.

However, in the forty-second fascicle of the *En’ōshō*, regarding the verse of homage at the beginning of the "Chapter on the Wheel of Transformation," it states: "I take refuge in the bodhicitta," etc. These six subsequent lines praise the Sanskrit original and appear within the *Sōjō Dai-nichi Ken-in* (The Great Sun Sword Seal of Monk Sōjō); they are most extremely secret.
The *Vairocana-tathāgata-bodhicitta-stotra* recorded here by the three masters Jue, Huiyun, and Zongrui is this very work.
Neither of these two versions contains the Sanskrit original; it is likely that it was omitted during transcription, though one might further seek out a separate edition.
